answer: That error almost always means HDF5 cannot load the compression filter at read time, not that the file is corrupt. Your image datasets are compressed with Blosc2, which is registered by the hdf5plugin package; the filter only exists in processes that have imported hdf5plugin. When it is missing, HDF5 falls back to searching its dynamic plugin directory (e.g. /usr/local/hdf5/lib/plugin), cannot open it, and raises OSError: Can't synchronously read data (can't open directory). Fix: in the reading script or notebook, import hdf5plugin before slicing (importing h5py alone is not enough): import h5py, hdf5plugin; f = h5py.File('video_prediction_224_testing.h5', 'r'); arr = f['trainval/image_log'][0]. Alternatively set the HDF5_PLUGIN_PATH environment variable to hdf5plugin.PLUGIN_PATH. Also note the datasets live inside groups, so index f['trainval/image_log'] and f['test/image_log'], not f['image_log']. A quick confirmation: the uncompressed pv_log/pv_pred float64 datasets will read fine without the import, while the compressed ones fail.

Your annotation is essentially correct; this is a PyCharm inference limitation. With typ: type[T] | tuple[type[T], ...] and a call passing (SomeLexemeSubclass, AnotherLexemeSubclass), the checker has to solve one T that covers both elements. The proper solution is the union T = SomeLexemeSubclass | AnotherLexemeSubclass, since (type[A], type[B]) is assignable to tuple[type[A | B], ...], and the function then returns list[A | B]. Mypy and pyright infer exactly that; PyCharm's solver refuses to join different type arguments across tuple elements and reports the spurious error. Workarounds: annotate an intermediate variable, e.g. types: tuple[type[A | B], ...] = (A, B), and pass that; or add overloads for the tuple case; or suppress the inspection with a noinspection comment. You could also type the parameter like typeshed types isinstance (a recursive, non-generic ClassInfo alias) and return list[Lexeme], but you lose element-type precision. Best practice: verify with mypy or pyright and trust them over PyCharm here.

This is a limitation of BPTK-Py's operator overloading, not your math. Element ** number is supported because it builds an expression-tree node, but element ** element is not implemented in your version, so the variable exponent silently degrades and you get 1.0. NumPy cannot help: Converter is not array-like and has no log method, hence the ufunc TypeError; you must stay inside BPTK's own DSL. Options: (1) If the exponent is effectively a constant (6 years), use a literal: Resale_Value_DM2.equation = Resale_Value_DM1 ** 6, or precompute the whole factor in Python ((1 - 0.0708) ** 6 = 0.643658) and assign it to a constant. (2) Rewrite a ** b as exp(b * ln(a)) using BPTK's sd_functions module if your version provides exp/log (check BPTK_Py.sddsl.functions); do not use numpy functions. (3) Compute the series outside the model in pandas and feed it back as a lookup or exogenous converter. Also try upgrading BPTK-Py; newer releases extended operator support.

bash's 'required file not found' means the shebang interpreter path does not resolve in the final image. /usr/local/bin/sandworm is a script whose shebang points into the tool venv, and that venv's bin/python is a symlink chain ending at the interpreter uv used in the builder, typically a uv-managed CPython living outside /usr/local. COPY copies symlinks, not their targets, so the chain dangles even after you copied /root/.local/share/uv. Diagnose in the builder: readlink -f /root/.local/share/uv/tools/sandworm-build/bin/python, then COPY that real interpreter directory into the final stage at the identical absolute path, alongside the tools dir and the shim. Cleaner: pin stable locations in the builder before installing, e.g. ENV UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR=/python UV_TOOL_DIR=/opt/uv-tools UV_TOOL_BIN_DIR=/opt/uv-bin, run uv tool install ., then in the gcc stage COPY --from=builder /python /python and /opt/uv-tools and /opt/uv-bin, adding /opt/uv-bin to PATH. Alternatively skip uv tool entirely: uv venv /opt/sandworm && uv pip install --python /opt/sandworm/bin/python /app, and copy /opt/sandworm plus the interpreter it links to.

This is Streamlit's rerun model, not a logic bug. Clicking Activate MFA triggers a complete rerun of the script from the top, and only during that rerun does form_submit_button return True. Your activate_mfa is almost certainly reached through a transient condition in the login flow, typically something like if st.button('Login'):. st.button returns True only on the single rerun immediately after it is clicked; on the next rerun, caused by the form submit, it is False again, so activate_mfa is never called at all, and everything from the if on line 24 onward appears to be skipped. The widget values are fine; the code path simply is not executed. Fix: persist the flow stage in st.session_state instead of gating on a button's return value. On successful password check set st.session_state.stage = 'mfa_setup'; at top level call activate_mfa(login) whenever stage == 'mfa_setup'; inside if submit: verify the OTP against st.session_state.sec_key (e.g. pyotp), update the database, set stage = 'logged_in', and call st.rerun().

Return the color from the model via Qt.ItemDataRole.BackgroundRole and skip the custom delegate. Both approaches are equally lazy: the view only requests data for and paints visible cells, so neither touches the whole DataFrame. But the model approach is what the default delegate already supports; it queries BackgroundRole and fills the cell correctly, cooperating with selection highlighting and styles. Your delegate version does strictly more work: super().paint() draws the item, then fillRect paints a translucent rectangle over it (overdraw, and the tint lands on top of the text), and index.data() calls back into your model anyway, so you pay the same lookup plus an extra pass. Memory is identical since nothing is stored; you can cache the two QColor objects as module constants instead of constructing them per call. If you ever do need a delegate, subclass QStyledItemDelegate (QItemDelegate is legacy) and set option.backgroundBrush in initStyleOption rather than painting manually. For large frames, the real cost is data() being called several times per visible cell, so keep it cheap (iat lookups, minimal formatting).

Add an autouse fixture in your top-level conftest.py so every test is checked automatically: import pytest; @pytest.fixture(autouse=True) def fail_on_output(capfd): yield; out, err = capfd.readouterr(); assert out == '' and err == '', f'stray output: {out!r} {err!r}'. Use capfd rather than capsys so writes that bypass sys.stdout (C extensions, os.write on fd 1/2) are caught as well; add --capture=fd to addopts to enforce fd-level capture. One nuance: the assertion fires during fixture teardown, so pytest reports it as an ERROR rather than a FAILURE; that still fails the run/CI, but if you want genuine failures, record the captured text and assert from a pytest_runtest_makereport hookwrapper instead. For stdin: while capturing is active pytest already replaces sys.stdin with a DontReadFromInput object that raises on any read, so that part comes for free. Guarding OS-level fd 0 is trickier; in the same fixture you can os.dup fd 0 away and dup2 the read end of a closed pipe (or devnull for plain EOF) over it, restoring in teardown.

Prefer merge, or its idiomatic cousin set_index + compare. The manual approach compares positionally after isin/sort/reset_index, which silently assumes ids are unique, both frames end up with exactly the same rows, and dtypes match; duplicate ids, missing rows, or NaNs produce misaligned comparisons with no warning. merge aligns rows by key explicitly, lets you handle one-sided ids (how='inner' vs 'outer' with indicator=True), and is vectorized C code, so it is also fast on large frames. Two refinements: (1) the most idiomatic form of what you want is df1.set_index('id').compare(df2.set_index('id')) after restricting both to the shared ids and columns; it returns only the differing cells labeled self/other. (2) In the merge version, compare null-safely: NaN != NaN, so use (a == b) | (a.isna() & b.isna()) rather than plain equality (your fillna approach works but can conflate a real value with the sentinel). Avoid Python-level row loops in either approach; column-wise vectorized comparisons are fine.

Two separate problems. First, resetting the password does not require reinstalling or SMTP: pgAdmin stores accounts in the SQLite file named by SQLITE_PATH, in your case /var/lib/pgadmin4/pgadmin4.db. setup.py only prompts for email/password when that file does not exist, which is why you only saw 'pgadmin4 application initialisation'. So keep (restore) config_local.py, stop the service, sudo rm /var/lib/pgadmin4/pgadmin4.db and the sessions directory, then run python3 venv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/pgadmin4/setup.py again; it will recreate the db and ask for new credentials. Deleting config_local.py was counterproductive: it just makes pgAdmin use the default db under ~/.pgadmin. Second, true removal: you have both apt and pip/venv installs. Run sudo apt purge 'pgadmin4*' && sudo apt autoremove (purge deletes config, remove does not), then delete leftovers: /usr/pgadmin4, /var/lib/pgadmin4, /var/log/pgadmin4, the whole venv directory (rm -rf venv), the Apache conf (sudo a2disconf pgadmin4), and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/pgadmin4*.list. pip uninstall 'succeeds' but leaves all that state behind, which is why it looked like nothing worked.

Your code is fine; the crash happens while importing mega.py's dependencies. mega.py pulls in an old tenacity whose async module still uses the @asyncio.coroutine decorator, which was removed in Python 3.11, hence the AttributeError on import. Fixes, in order of preference: (1) Upgrade tenacity in place: pip install -U tenacity (versions >= 8 no longer touch asyncio.coroutine, and mega.py's retry usage works with them). If pip resists because of mega.py's pin, do pip install --upgrade --no-deps tenacity, or install mega.py with --no-deps and add requests, pycryptodome and tenacity yourself. (2) Run under Python 3.10 or older, where asyncio.coroutine still exists. (3) Longer term, note mega.py has been unmaintained since about 2020; consider a maintained fork on PyPI/GitHub or MEGA's official MEGAcmd/SDK for anything serious, because after this import error you may still hit API changes (login and request handling) that an abandoned client will not track.

A paid tier is not the core issue; the free tier can attach media, but video must go through the full chunked upload state machine, and 'media IDs are invalid' usually means part of it was skipped. Required flow: (1) INIT with media_type=video/mp4, total_bytes, and crucially media_category=tweet_video; without the category, video processing/attachment fails. (2) APPEND the file in chunks (up to ~5 MB each) with segment_index. (3) FINALIZE. (4) If FINALIZE returns processing_info, poll STATUS until state == 'succeeded'; attaching before processing completes is the classic cause of this error, and 1.8 MB is far below any size limit. (5) Post with the v2 endpoint using the string id: json={'text': ..., 'media': {'media_ids': [media_id_string]}} with the same OAuth 1.0a user context, and ensure the app has Read and Write permission (regenerate access tokens after changing it). Also note X deprecated upload.twitter.com/1.1/media/upload.json in 2025; if you get 404/410 there, switch to https://api.x.com/2/media/upload, which follows the same INIT/APPEND/FINALIZE/STATUS flow.

journal_mode cannot be changed inside a transaction, and with autocommit=False the sqlite3 module keeps one open at all times (it issues BEGIN at connect and again after every commit), so on that connection the PRAGMA can never run. The key realization: WAL is a persistent property of the database file, not of the connection. You only need to set it once, and all later connections inherit it. So set it from a separate short-lived connection opened in autocommit mode before creating your main connection: tmp = sqlite3.connect(db_path, autocommit=True); tmp.execute('PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL'); tmp.close(); then db = sqlite3.connect(db_path, autocommit=False) as usual. You can even do it in a one-off migration script rather than app startup. If a second connection is truly impossible, the alternative is flipping the attribute temporarily: db.commit(); db.autocommit = True; db.execute('PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL'); db.autocommit = False; changing the attribute mid-connection is supported and ends the implicit transaction. Connection-local pragmas like synchronous are unaffected and can stay where they are.

The two machines are not running the same Cython: 0.29.37 works, 3.1.2 fails; the OS/Python difference is mostly a red herring. Cython 3.x generates different C code, and some helper symbols (your __pyx_CommonTypesMetaclass_get_module among them) are emitted into every generated translation unit in a way that is not safely combinable, so when you compile several Cython-generated .c files and link them into one binary, the linker sees duplicate definitions. Easiest fix: pin the same Cython everywhere; on the Kubuntu 20.04 machine run python3 -m pip install 'cython==0.29.37' (or any <3.0), regenerate the C files, and your existing GCC flow works unchanged. If you want to stay on Cython 3, do not link multiple generated modules into a single image naively: build each module as its own shared extension, and look at Cython 3's shared utility/module support for factoring out common code; also regenerate all C files with one identical Cython version. Note that -fcommon tricks will not help, since that only affects tentative variable definitions, not functions.

'Couldn't connect' means nothing is listening on the port: the container almost certainly never reached the point where uvicorn binds 8000. Check docker ps (is the container even still running?) and docker logs -f <container>. Two likely causes given your setup: (1) Module path mismatch. The Dockerfile does COPY app ./app and runs uvicorn app.main:app, which requires your code to be at ./app/main.py on the host (ideally with app/__init__.py). If your file actually sits in the project root or has another name, uvicorn exits immediately with 'Could not import module app.main' and the port never opens; the fix is to match the layout or change the CMD to yourmodule:app. (2) Startup time and memory. pipeline('zero-shot-classification', model='joeddav/xlm-roberta-large-xnli') downloads a multi-GB model at import time; until that finishes uvicorn is not listening, and Docker Desktop's default memory limit can OOM-kill the container mid-load. Wait for 'Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000' in the logs before testing, pre-download the model during docker build, raise the memory limit, and drop --reload in containers.
